utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I have the appearances for the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, Mr. Dan Saxon, Ms. Melissa Pack. My name is Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and with us is Ana Katalinic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: As assigned counsel, David Hooper, with Dr. Andreas O'Shea, assisted by Lea Kulinowski, who is our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hooper. The accused is not present. During a Pre-Trial Conference held this morning, this Chamber was informed about why he is not present. The Chamber has, on its mind, to proceed even where the accused is absent. Before, however, finally deciding to do so, if any of the parties would like to make any submissions on this matter, they are invited to do so. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: This morning, we understand that the Prosecution are due to present their opening of the case, and that is a matter which Dr. Seselj can see from the transcript or video or audio that he would doubtless be provided with, and we take no objection at all in those circumstances. We do raise concerns as to the medical health of Dr. Seselj. He's no longer a young man. We understand that he has in the past, as a result of activities in Serbia or former Yugoslavia, suffered periods of imprisonment where he has, in fact, engaged in hunger strikes, and some of them have gone on for quite a long time. He's no longer that young man. We are concerned about his health. We understand that he is being seen by a Dr. Falke at the Detention Unit. We would be particularly concerned that, for example, his weight loss is something that is attended to or has regard -- has regard to, and is something which you, the Judges, are provided with some information. Because my understanding is that in a hunger strike or an absence of food, as the Registry, we heard, would nominate it, that in such circumstances, one of the key factors is loss of weight and the attended risks to health that poses. I don't know what regime is presently in place for the Chamber to be made aware of Dr. Seselj's position. We understand that there was certainly a daily report provided to the Registry, and we assume that comes to you, the Judges. Those are all my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hooper. I do understand that you take no objection to the Chamber proceeding in the absence of the accused, at least for today, as you said. I'll later say a few words about the other submissions you've made -- you made. Before delivering a decision of the Chamber to proceed in the absence of the accused, I do understand that the Prosecution will start giving its opening statement. I'm not certain, Mr. Hooper, about where Mr. Seselj earlier expressed that he would like to postpone his opening statement until a later stage and only to make an unsworn statement, whether that's the course you have in mind as well, which would mean that once we had heard the opening statement by the Prosecution, that we'd then, at least if Mr. Seselj would be present in court tomorrow, that we'd then hear an unsworn statement from him, unless you, now as assigned counsel, would like to make an opening statement or whether you'd follow the earlier course decided by Mr. Seselj to delay an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Of course, the Defence have the option of making an opening statement now or deferring it just before the defence case, under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I wouldn't at this stage assume, even if I was in a position to do so, which I'm not, to make an opening statement. I wouldn't make that opening statement now because to do so would intrude, I think, over much into Dr. Seselj's position, and his right to make such an opening statement at an appropriate time can be preserved in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that Mr. Seselj, of course, under the supervision of the Chamber, can make an unsworn statement at the beginning, but his right to make an opening statement, I would say the Defence has a right to make an opening statement, because, since this morning, Mr. Seselj is not in a position anymore to address directly this Chamber. Of course, if he wants to participate in it, he can ask, through you, for permission to do so. So for the time being, the Chamber could expect that after the opening statement of the Prosecution, that either we hear an unsworn statement of Mr. Seselj, or if he doesn't appear and if he doesn't want to make such an unsworn statement, that we'd then proceed and start hearing evidence early December.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. Our position at the moment is, as the Chamber, I'm sure, is aware, that there's been no contact, absolutely no contact between ourselves and Dr. Seselj, and I see no imminent change in that position. We will seek to make contact with him this afternoon. I understand that it's anticipated that the Prosecution opening may not conclude today. I don't know if I'm correct about that. But we'll see in any event. But if that's the case, then we will obviously go over until tomorrow, where, in any event, court time is allocated, and perhaps we can generally re-address the position, not that I feel for a moment that I'd be in a position to make an opening statement, but we can re-address the position tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: -- perhaps in the light of our inquiries today. And obviously Dr. Seselj will be invited, if there is a hearing again tomorrow, to attend this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: And we'll see if he takes that opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber can only confirm that Mr. Seselj, of course, is not only entitled, but that the Chamber even would prefer him to be present at trial, because that would better serve the interests of justice. That being clarified, I informed the parties that if we might run out of time today, of course, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, then you'll be in a position to continue tomorrow. Tomorrow we have not the full morning session available to ourselves. We have to stop a bit earlier, after the -- before the second break, approximately. If need be, since Mr. Seselj has been attributed a certain amount of time as well, we would then continue Friday, in the afternoon, not Wednesday, not Thursday. Then I'll deliver the decision of this Chamber to proceed in the absence of the accused. The Chamber establishes that the accused is aware of this trial to start. The accused has put forward claims, although not by himself directly addressing this Chamber, claims including that the Chamber changes certain decisions it previously took. Among these decisions, there are some for which a legal avenue to challenge them was or still is open to the accused. Apparently, the accused wants to put pressure to have his claims honoured by his refusal to take any food offered by the United Nations Detention Unit, which has resulted in, as the Chamber understands, a deterioration of his health. The absence of the accused is thus caused by, if not a deliberate decision not to appear, by a self-induced weak physical condition and cannot be accepted by this Chamber as a reason to postpone the start of this trial. In addition to this decision, the Chamber regrets that the accused is not present at the start of this trial, as I said before. The Chamber further expresses its concerns about consequences of the accused's decision to refuse to take food provided by the UNDU and not to take his medication, consequences unfavourable to his physical condition. Finally, the Chamber encourages the accused to choose legal avenues if he seeks to challenge any decision this Trial Chamber takes or has taken. In response to one of your questions, Mr. Hooper, the Chamber has invited the Registrar to keep the Chamber, at regular intervals, to keep acquainted with any development in relation to the physical condition of the accused. If there's any need to further discuss that in this courtroom, we'll hear either from you or from the Prosecution or take the initiative ourselves. The Chamber stresses, however, that the first responsible authority for medical care to be provided to those who are detained in the Detention Unit is the Registrar of this Tribunal. Then, having dealt with these preliminary matters, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, I'd like to invite you to make the opening statement on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, this case has its origin in the process of the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia and the emergence of new independent states, among them Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is a case about Serb leaders, among them the accused Vojislav Seselj, in Serbia and Montenegro, as well as in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, who resisted this process and insisted that their vision of a state for all Serbs, or a new Yugoslavia, or, as the accused said, a Greater Serbia, must prevail no matter what the cost. As it became increasingly less likely that they would achieve their objectives by negotiations, these leaders resorted to the politics of violence, often invoking old historical grudges and wrongs to instil fear and hatred in their people and incite them to violence against their neighbours. Their ethnocentric politics became the politics of separation where the suffering of the enemies, namely, the Croat and the Muslim populations, as well as other non-Serbs, was viewed as a harsh but necessary cost of achieving their goal of a new Serbian state. The events themselves were notorious and the term "ethnic cleansing" came into common use. Let me quote from Exhibit 429, a report of the Special Rapporteur of the UN Commission on Human Rights, dated 27 October, 1992. Your Honour, my colleague, Ms. Katalinic, will always show you the exhibits I talk about on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have no exhibits yet. I take it we have, until now, ERN numbers. Whenever you introduce -- at least that's my understanding, but I'm new in e-court as well. But as soon as you introduce any document, that it will be given an identifying number later to become an exhibit number once the exhibit has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, today we have no e-court. Today, we actually go with Sanction, so you would have to press, actually, which button? ELMO, the ELMO button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I was under the misapprehension that we would start immediately in e-court, but we'll start only on the second day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So if you press the ELMO ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had some practical problems, but they are resolved now. Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Sorry to interfere. It may have been a matter I should have raised right at the outset, but with Dr. Seselj not being here, my understanding is that there are facilities, if he wishes to avail himself of them, to follow the proceedings today. I don't know if that extends to exhibits. I understand there's a videostream which can be accessed from a distance. I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was offered to Mr. Seselj, as far as I remember, is that where he earlier received videos of the proceedings, that at least video coverage of the proceedings, which would include everything that's shown on the ELMO, is made available to him. That does not necessarily mean that he can always keep them under his own control, and this is raised by some security concerns envisaged by the Registrar. But at least what now appears on our screens is accessible to Mr. Seselj as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You see on your screens the report of the Special Rapporteur of the UN Commission on Human Rights, dated the 27th October, 1992. In paragraph 6, he states that "the principal objective of the military conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the establishment of ethnically homogeneous regions. Ethnic cleansing does not appear to be the consequence of the war, but rather the goal. This goal, to a large extent, has already been achieved through killings, beatings, rape, destruction of houses and threats." This part of the report refers to Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, in the same report, in paragraph 17, the unbearable living conditions in Sarajevo are mentioned, a mass grave in Vukovar is mentioned in paragraph 18, and ethnic cleansing of non-Serbs in Vojvodina at paragraph 22 of that same report. I will come to these events later. Vojislav Seselj, along with others, pursued the goal of a new homogeneous Serbian state through a massive state-sponsored persecution campaign in parts of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in Serbia itself, including killing, detention, deportation or forcible transfer, plunder, destruction of religious sites, and razing of entire villages and settlements. The accused in this case, Vojislav Seselj, was and is a politician, a well-educated, a professor, a shrewd and calculating man, an extreme Serb nationalist, a master of political manipulation masked with patriotic rhetoric. He said about himself the following during his testimony in the Milosevic case, and I refer here to our Exhibit 2828, at the session of the 31st August, 2005. He said: "There is no greater scandalmonger in Serbian political life than me over the past 15 years. When I needed this kind of scandal out of political interests, I was the one who could do that the most skillfully." You'll find that at T43500. He also admitted during the cross-examination in that case that he would resort to untruths when waging a political propaganda war. You'll find that at page 43807 and 43443. He even admitted that many of his statements during the events relevant to the indictment may have resembled warmongering, and you'll find that quote at 43385 of the transcript of the Milosevic case. Let me show you how Vojislav Seselj often presented himself during the events. You see him here wearing a Serbian hat with a kokarda and a rifle. This is Exhibit 632. During the events relevant to the indictment, the accused was the president of the Serbian Radical Party, the SRS. He was a charismatic face of an ultra-nationalist policy that promoted a homogeneous Greater Serbia, with its western borders along the infamous Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. In addition, Vojislav Seselj was the head of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, the SCP, a movement that, according to the statute of the SRS party, was a collective member of this party and became the military wing of the SRS during the conflict. In fact, one can call it the party army. Seselj called himself in an order, that you see here on your screen, order 124 of the 13th May 1993, he calls himself "the only Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda directly engaged in the ongoing liberation movement of the Serbian people, following in the tradition of the Serbian Chetniks." On the last page of that same document, he signs as the President of the Central Homeland Administration of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, the highest organ of the movement. That's Exhibit 2015. The SRS/SCP volunteers, in fact, considered him to be their commander. In this case, you will hear evidence from witnesses and see documents about the various individuals and organs of the SRS and the SCP, both in Belgrade and in the regions, and how they took part in the events. I will address some of these structures and individuals when speaking about specific locations. At this point just this, the evidence will show that despite the organs that were set up in the SRS party and the SCP movement, there was only one leader of both and that was Vojislav Seselj. The accused would be informed of the smallest details of these organs -- by these organs, and only he would make the decisions. He was an autocrat by nature and made decisions independently. When communicating with persons from the party or the movement, he would always do so in raised voice, making it obvious that what he was proposing had to be executed no matter what. In this case, the Prosecution will prove that together with others Vojislav Seselj implemented policies to expel non-Serbs from territories claimed to be Serbian lands. The accused not only promoted the expulsion of non-Serbs from specific targeted territories and incited his audience to do so, in addition, he recruited and indoctrinated volunteers and set up a party army that pursued this course brutally. Through his extreme rhetorics, the accused attracted many young men who volunteered and became part of the thousands of SRS volunteers who participated in the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, many of them undisciplined, violent and even criminal. The Prosecution will lead evidence, both in writing and orally, showing how the radical speeches of the accused affected not only volunteers associated with the SRS or the SCP, but also other volunteers, reservists, regular soldiers of the JNA and the VJ, and local Serbs, instilling in them fear and hatred. In addition, we will hear that the radical speeches had also a strong immediate effect on the non-Serbs who listened to them. Hearing the accused and his threats was enough to many of the non-Serbs to leave their homes, fearing for their lives. My colleague, Mr. Saxon, will address these aspects of the accused's criminal conduct in more details later on. However, this case is not only about the accused's words. The accused and his associates in the SRS and the SCP party -- SCP movement took part in the financing, supply, transfer, and direction of the actions of the volunteers participating with other Serb forces in the persecution of non-Serbs. In this trial you will hear evidence and receive documentation that despite the subordination of these volunteers under the regular military commanders in the field, the volunteers often stayed together in units commanded by SRS company, detachment or squad leaders who would report back not only to the regular military command on the front lines but also to the accused and his associates in the party offices in Belgrade. The criminal charges against Vojislav Seselj in the Redacted Modified Amended Indictment are three counts of crimes against humanity, those being persecution, deportation and inhumane acts-forcible transfer; and six counts of violations of the laws and customs of war, those being murder, torture, cruel treatment, wanton destruction of villages or devastation, destruction or wilful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion and plunder. The Prosecution alleges that the accused, under Article 7(1) of the Statute, is responsible for the crimes listed because he planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted their planning, preparation or execution. As far as the term "committed" is used, the Prosecution alleges that the accused physically committed the crimes of persecution, that's count 1, by direct and public incitement and denigration with respect to his speeches in Vukovar, Mali Zvornik, and Hrtkovci; and also counts 10 and 11, deportation and forcible transfer, with respect to his speech in Hrtkovci. In addition, when using the term "committed," the Prosecution refers to his participation in a joint criminal enterprise, the objective of which was the permanent forcible removal of Croat, Muslims and other non-Serbs from large areas of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina claimed to be Serbian through the commission of crimes. The Prosecution will present evidence that the specific crimes identified in the indictment were within the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution's position is that the crimes of deportation and forcible transfer constituted the JCE's common objective from the very start. Whether the other crimes, such as murder, detention, torture, beatings, sexual assaults and destructions of property, were originally -- were original to the objective of the JCE from the very start or added later due to the circumstances on the ground is irrelevant. The Prosecution will prove that these crimes were adopted by the JCE members during the events and incorporated into the criminal plan. The evidence will show that the common objective of the JCE never changed, but that the implementation of this common objective evolved, and as a matter of fact, all the crimes charged in the indictment became part of the criminal means through which the JCE pursued its goal throughout the period relevant to the indictment. The indictment alleges, alternatively, that the crimes enumerated in some of the counts of the indictment were the natural and foreseeable consequences of the execution of the JCE and that Vojislav Seselj was fully aware of the horrific consequences that the implementation of the objective of the JCE would bring to the non-Serb population in the targeted areas. To this end, let me quote from an interview he gave on the 24th of May, 1991, and I refer here to Exhibit 569. He said, after returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina, where he inter alia had met Radovan Karadzic, the following: "We have already deployed several Chetniks groups in Zagreb and other towns across Croatia, which are trained in sabotage and terrorist activities. If Serbian civilians start to be massacred, the Chetniks will strike at Zagreb and other concentrations of Croats, using their full strength. You know, when one retaliates, revenge is blind. There would be innocent victims, but what can you do. Let the Croats think about that first. We shall not strike first, but if they should strike, we are not even going to bother where our blows land. Also, unless the army disarms the Ustashas immediately, there will be a lot of blood." "And in a Radio B-92 interview, on the 30th of September, 1993," and I refer here to Exhibit 772, "a listener asks whether Seselj ever worries about the non-Serbian population that is innocent and suffering due to his views, and Seselj answers: 'Why would I have a guilty conscience? So many innocent Serbs suffered in this war, and I need to worry about those who belong to another enemy people, if possibly there was an innocent one among them that suffered. You know, in war one experiences great turmoil, great troubles, and I, in war, above all, worry about those who belong to my own people.'" Vojislav Seselj participated in the joint criminal enterprise together with all the individuals and groups listed in paragraph 8 of the indictment. It was a vast JCE, including a large group of persons. There was a core group of JCE members in Belgrade, including politicians, such as the accused and Slobodan Milosevic, members of the SFRY Presidency, high-ranking officials of the JNA and the VJ and the Serbian MUP. There were also core groups in specific regions, such as in the SAO Krajina in Croatia, including Milan Martic and Milan Babic, who pled guilty in this Tribunal; and in the SAO Eastern Slavonia, you have the core group Baranja and Western Srem - sorry - you have the core group including Goran Hadzic, Radovan Stojicic, better known by his nickname Badza, and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you had the core group, including Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Biljana Plavsic, who also pled guilty here in this Tribunal. There were also local components of the JCE in the municipalities, including Zeljko Raznjatovic, better known as Arkan, and the so-called Vojvodas, the latter all close associates of the accused. I will give more details regarding these local components of the JCE later when I address the regions. The Prosecution is not in a position, nor is it necessary in this case, to identify all the members of the JCE by name. What the evidence will show is that the accused was a member in it and sufficiently connected and concerned with persons who committed the crimes in pursuit of the common objective or who engaged other perpetrators to do so. By now, the history of the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia is well known, and I do not want to spend much time on this. I also do not want to address the details of the implementation of the structures of the JCE in the targeted regions. Insofar, I refer to the Prosecution's brief where all the details are laid out. Instead, I will review with you the goals of the JCE as they relate to certain territories, in particular, the goals of this accused and how they evolved due to major political events. Vojislav Seselj left no doubt about what his goal was at the beginning of the conflict. It was a homogeneous Greater Serbia. We will hear and see a lot of evidence to this effect. Seselj himself called this idea of Greater Serbia the raison d'etre of the SRS till the present day, and I refer here to his testimony in the Milosevic case, at page 42887. The territory of Greater Serbia is described by the accused in many speeches, of which I will only give one, and it's the speech of the 4th of August, 1990, and it's Exhibit 776. And I quote: "But, we are warning them that never, at any cost, will we allow this Croatian state to be established covering the Serbian population. We will never allow any Serbian territory, any Serbian settlement, destroyed church or torched village, any Serbian mass grave, camp, pit, slaughterhouse, to find itself beyond the borders of the Serbian state." And a bit later, he said, during that same speech: "We always proceed from the Croatian people being the one that marked the borders of the Serbian state. Marking them with Serbian mass graves." And he further said, referring to Tudjman's election victory in Croatia, he said the following: "That victory has shown that the vast majority of the Croatian people are with the Ustasha movement, just as the Croats had massively welcomed and supported Pavelica's regime in WWII. We have no illusions regarding the Croatian national nature, we have no illusions regarding their ultimate goals. Therefore, we won't even negotiate with them. For these negotiations and rotten compromises have always been at the expense of the Serbian national interests. We, regarding our territories and regarding our graves, will not negotiate with anyone in this wide world." Let me show you now the platform of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and it's Exhibit 2018. In the programme of the Serbian Chetnik Movement in 1990, among the goals we find under (i), the restoration of a free, independent and democratic Serbian state in the Balkans which will include all Serbian people and all Serbian territories, including the Republic of Serbia, Serbian Macedonia, Serbian Montenegro, Serbian Bosnia, Serbian Herzegovina, Serbian Dubrovnik, Serbian Lika, Serbian Kordun, Serbian Banija, Serbian Slavonia, and Serbian Baranja. An almost identical first goal is formulated in the SRS Manifesto of February 1991. You find it here in the -- it's Exhibit 2019, and you find it here in -- as the first goal, and you find actually it's absolutely the same text except for one change. Added in the list of territories is also now "Serbian Dalmatia," right after Dubrovnik, you find Serbian Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd allow me to interfere for one second. You started reading a portion of it, and then you left out two or three lines and then you read the last couple of lines. Perhaps it would be good if you take several portions of a text you read, Mr. Seselj, if he would review the video, could not follow the English, that you make clear that these are separate portions and that it's not one portion you're reading, so to say I leave out a couple of lines, I continue them. Best would be to read all of it so that the context is not lost if Mr. Seselj listens to the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to the speech that he gave or rather to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, to the -- you said the goals we find number 1, and then the restoration of a free, independent, and democratic Serbian state, and then you left out a couple of lines and then you -- and that's not clear, when reading or listening to you, that you did not read two lines "imposed upon us," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will do that, yes. Vojislav Seselj, in his many speeches, referred to the western borders of the Serbian state as the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. And you see here a map, and it's Exhibit 1891, and you see the black line. That's actually a line that connects these places that I just mentioned, and it shows actually the territory that the accused had in mind when he was speaking about Greater Serbia with these western borders. The accused and his associates did not only claim territory in which Serbs constituted the majority population, but also areas such as Dubrovnik and other locations in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina where Serbs were in a minority. To this end, the Serb suffering during the Second World War was utilised by the accused and others not only to instil fear in the Serb people, but also to revoke a birthright to certain so-called historical lands. The accused himself, during the testimony in the Milosevic case, and I refer here to transcript 437 -- 43275, said the following: "The SRS made a geographical map of Greater Serbia, and from that map, which we published countless times on the cover page of the colour back side of our magazine, one can say that the western borders of the Greater Serbia is on the Karlobag-Ogulin-Virovitica line. That does not contain only territories where Serbs are in the majority. It contains also many territories where Croats, Macedonians and Muslims are majority populations." Not accidentally is the map with the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line very similar to the territories of the old Serbian Chetnik -- that the old Serbian Chetnik Movement pursued before during the First and the Second World War. And you can see here a map of Greater Serbia that our technical people actually put into the regular time smack of the Balkans, and you can see that it is basically the same that was published on the back side of the magazine of the party organ, Velika Srbija. And here, this map will later be Exhibit 2004. The accused and his followers saw themselves as successors of this old Serbian Nationalist Movement. In relation to the volunteers of the SRS, a document, "Basic Military Organs of the Serbian Radical Party Volunteers," you'll see here, adopted by the SRS Main Board in June 1991. That's Exhibit 1261. And I refer here only to paragraph 3, where it says: "The volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party are continuing the honourable patriotic traditions of the volunteers and Chetniks of the Serbian liberation rebellions, uprisings and wars until the end of 1918; Chetnik organisation 1902-1918; and Serbian Chetniks in World War II ..." This text, of course, continues. The Prosecution will present evidence, including expert testimony, on what this old nationalist movement stood for, namely, an aggressive and violent pursuit of a homogeneous Serbian state. Other members of the JCE did not use the term "Greater Serbia." Witness evidence will show that Slobodan Milosevic insisted that Serbs remain in one state, and stated that divisions of Yugoslavia into several states which would separate Serbian people and force them to live in separate sovereign states of others would be out of the question. Milosevic officially seemed to have been in favour of the old Yugoslavia during parts of 1991. For the accused Seselj, Federal Yugoslavia was only an interim solution in the struggle for a Greater Serbia. However, by June 1991, Milosevic and the Serbian and Montenegrin members of the SFRY Presidency were pursuing the creation of a new Serbian state and were discussing the redeployment of the JNA along the new Serbian borders of the Yugoslavia. As Borisav Jovic put it in his book, "the last days of the SFRY," it will become Exhibit 1869. He also wrote in this book: "By working to destroy and break up Yugoslavia, Croatia and Bosnia themselves are working to create a Greater Serbia." Let me show another map. I have here a map. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, I'm trying to follow your maps as well. May I draw your attention to the following: You seem to have taken over what I consider, personally, a bad habit by the Prosecution, that is, to use projected maps at the same time as -- if you look at map 14 and 15, although you'll see that it's the same area, one is projected and the other is giving a real picture. It makes it completely impossible to do any measurement on maps which are projected. Therefore, to the extent possible, could you please provide us with non-projected maps, and just the ones that look from top to bottom and not from a certain angle, which really changes all the dimensions. I hope you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm not really sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at 14 and 15, on 14 you get a real map as you would find it whatever -- the other one, you see all the dimensions are quite different. North/south becomes smaller; east/west becomes larger. That's because of a certain projection technique which is used. In that way, all the maps of Bosnia and Herzegovina start looking different. For example, you'll find the same two maps before that. You also have this projected one of strategic objectives, which makes it very difficult to compare maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd give it some attention, some thought, not to act upon it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, for this remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So this is now a map that was published on the 22nd of October, 1991, in the magazine Epoha, and it is Exhibit 2880. This is a map that relates to the targeted territory for the new Serb dominated Yugoslavia pursued at that time, in October 1991, by the Serbian leadership around Slobodan Milosevic. There is Cyrillic text in this, but I can assist you in finding your way in this map. If you look at the territory indicated as number 1, that indicates the SAO Krajina. When you look at number 2, that's Western Slavonia. Number 3 is SAO Western Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Number 4 is Western Herzegovina. Number 5 is the Posavina Corridor. Number 6 is the Dubrovnik Republic. And the curved line on -- at the most western part of the map, that's, again, the line -- the line Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line, and in this Epoha article, it's meant -- this line is called the optimal western borders of Serbian countries. That's, in October, what the plan of the JCE had evolved to. As can be seen from the map that Milosevic territory shows and the previous map of Greater Serbia, it's almost identical; it's, indeed, the same territory. The evidence will further show that the relevant time -- in the relevant time period, the JCE members in the regions in Croatia were fully in line with Slobodan Milosevic, as well as Vojislav Seselj. The evidence will show that the Serbian leaders in the SAOs in Croatia, in collaboration with the JCE members in Belgrade, set up the political, police, and military structures that engaged in a war for territory to create the western borders of the new state. One of those engaged was the accused, and he was personally present in these territories from the beginning to the end. He was present when, on the 25th of July, 1990, at a gathering in Srb, near Knin, Milan Babic and other SDS Krajina leaders established a Serb Assembly and a Serbian National Counsel and passed a declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serbian nation in Croatia. Vojislav Seselj was present during the first violent clashes in Plitvice in the SAO Krajina on 31 March 1991. Seselj's men were involved in the violence in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991, in Eastern Slavonia. The accused was present in Vukovar before it fell to the Serb forces and he was also present in Vocin in Western Slavonia. The evidence will show that he was in constant contact with the Croatian Serb leaderships in all the SAOs. The accused even supported Milan Babic by the end of 1991 in his opposition to the Vance plan, but later on Mr. Seselj then bent to the greater power, meaning Slobodan Milosevic. Let me briefly address the military leadership that participated in the JCE. The Prosecution will provide written and witness evidence that the military, namely, the JNA generals and the -- in the Main Staff, at the beginning of the disintegration of the Yugoslavia, were not in favour of a new Serbian state, but rather pursued the continuation of the old Yugoslavia. However, in July 1991, with Slovenia gone, Generals pressured by Milosevic and the Serbian and Montenegrin members of the Presidency, gave up the idea of the unitary Yugoslavia and moved their main forces to the future borders of the new Serb-dominated state along the lines just shown before. When the Serbian and Montenegrin leadership on the 1st of October, 1991, took over the SFRY Presidency and thus the Supreme Command of the JNA, the JNA sided openly with the Serbian leadership. In a report of the 1st of October, 1991 - and that's Exhibit 3009 - they warned the Croatian government and other organs that they would now retaliate for any Croatian military action. The events of the 1st October 1991 reveal the amount of coordination within the JCE; namely, on that same day, not only the Serbian leadership and the JNA leadership took actions, on that same day, the Montenegrin leadership acted in coordination and mobilised their special police unit for the attack on Dubrovnik which started the following day. And you can just -- I invite you to briefly look at the order of the 1st of October. It's Exhibit 3008, in which Momcilo Bulatovic actually mobilised the police for the attack on Dubrovnik. And the SRS in Belgrade acted as well. And here you see their decision, this is a decision of the 1st of October, 1991, from the -- from the SRS Crisis Staff. It's Exhibit 1959. In the minutes of this Crisis Staff meeting, it states: "Pursuant to proposals by Vojvoda V. Seselj and Mr. Ljubisa Petkovic, and in accordance with the current political situation in the country, it was decided to change the name of the SRS Crisis Staff into SRS war staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, this is not the second page of the document we saw before which was totally illegible to me. I don't know what you said, 3008, in which Mr. Bulatovic mobilised the police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that could be shown on your screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's number 1.

utterances.text: It's 1 and 2 together.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's actually the best. You see here, the mobilisation of the special police, and it's in 2, it's referred to the Dubrovnik front.

utterances.text: Yes, it's Mr. Bulatovic. And the other order, perhaps again, also the other order, if you see it, we can actually make it bigger, the whole -- it's not so difficult to read. It's actually minutes taken by the secretary of the SRS, and you see here, in paragraph 1, this reference that there would be now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That one was read to us, so we're able to follow that. But not the previous one.
